attacks.claim: The PR text promises that id tie-breaking keeps paging with --limit stable, but the diff has no offset or cursor. LIMIT is the only paging term, so --limit truncates and cannot page. The id tie-break only makes a single result set deterministic. The description must be corrected before merge.
attacks.evidence: "Ties are broken by transaction id so paging with --limit stays stable." vs. "LIMIT ?" with args (o.Account, o.Since.Unix(), o.Limit) and ABSENT: any offset or cursor field in listOpts or the flag set.

attacks.claim: The spec asks for a usage error, but the code returns a plain fmt.Errorf from buildListQuery. The message does list the valid keys and the check runs before any SQL executes. Cobra normally prints usage on RunE errors unless SilenceUsage is set, but the diff does not show the RunE wiring, so the exact output and exit code should be confirmed.
attacks.evidence: "return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid --sort %q (valid: %s)", o.SortKey, validSortKeys())" with ABSENT: any SilenceUsage or RunE change in the hunks.

attacks.claim: TestBuildListQuery only checks substrings of the query text and never runs SQL against SQLite. NOCASE ordering, the COALESCE category sort, the DESC id tie-break, and the valid-keys text in the error message are therefore unverified. There is also no category case and no DESC case for payee or category.
attacks.evidence: Cases: date, amount desc, payee, "amount; DROP TABLE transactions", empty key; check is "if err != nil || !strings.Contains(q, tc.want)"; ABSENT: DB-backed row-order test or error-text assertion.

attacks.claim: Non-date sorts (amount, payee, COALESCE category) cannot use an index, so SQLite sorts every matching row for the account before applying LIMIT. This is acceptable for a single-user local database, but it is unmeasured and no EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN note is given.
attacks.evidence: "ORDER BY %s %s, t.id %s" followed by "LIMIT ?"; ABSENT: CREATE INDEX or query-plan evidence.

attacks.claim: NULL ordering for amount_cents and payee is unstated. SQLite sorts NULLs first in ASC. COLLATE NOCASE folds only ASCII, so non-ASCII payee names will not sort case-insensitively. Neither behaviour is documented or tested.
attacks.evidence: "payee": "t.payee COLLATE NOCASE"; "amount": "t.amount_cents"; ABSENT: NULL or collation handling in the spec or tests.

attacks.claim: amount sorts on signed cents, so ASC lists the largest outflows first. The help text gives no direction semantics, so users may not get the order they expect.
attacks.evidence: "amount": "t.amount_cents" with help "sort key: "+validSortKeys(); no direction note.

attacks.claim: The --sort help text is a bare comma-separated list. It does not explain the keys, the default direction, or that --desc is needed for reverse order.
The category key goes beyond the request, which asked for amount and payee. It is also untested. Category sorting is therefore new public surface without coverage.
attacks.evidence: Request: "sort ... by amount or payee"; sortColumns includes "category": "COALESCE(c.name, '') COLLATE NOCASE"; the test table has no category case.

attacks.claim: SQL is assembled with fmt.Sprintf, so injection safety depends entirely on the sortColumns map being the only source of the column fragment. A future key added outside the map, or reuse of this pattern, could reintroduce injection. Only one injection case is tested.
attacks.evidence: "return fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT ... ORDER BY %s %s, t.id %s LIMIT ?`, col, dir, dir), nil"
